h1:
Breakfast Like a Trang Local
Roast Pork, Dim Sum & Old Coffee
intro: Mornings in Trang start before sunrise. Older generations had to head out to tap rubber by 4 or 5 a.m., so the tea shops and traditional coffee houses opened in the pre-dawn dark to catch them. People sit with a cloth-filtered coffee, order roast pork sliced into pieces, and fill the table with small steamer baskets of dim sum, chatting before the day begins. This is a breakfast culture that Trang pulls off better than any other town in the south. We picked the spots locals actually go to and that are still open right now, with areas, prices and hours, so you can wake up and land at the right table at the right time.

blocks.html: Trang's breakfast culture comes from the Chinese who settled here to farm rubber and trade more than a century ago, and they brought the kopitiam tea-house tradition with them. A Trang morning table usually has three things covered: Trang roast pork with crisp, fragrant skin, hot dim sum straight from the steamer, and cloth-filtered traditional coffee that's rich, sweet and creamy. We've split this into sections with real spots open right now, in case you want to eat breakfast the way locals genuinely do.

blocks.text: Trang Roast Pork — the Star of Breakfast

blocks.html: Trang roast pork is a whole side of pork belly, marinated and roasted in a traditional oven until the skin puffs up crisp and turns golden brown while the meat inside stays tender and juicy. What makes it special is that people in Trang eat roast pork for breakfast, not as an evening snack. You order it by the 100-gram serving, sliced onto a plate, dipped in sweet sauce or soy, eaten alongside traditional coffee and dim sum. Trang roast pork has earned Geographical Indication (GI) status and is one of those signature dishes you can only really get this way in Trang.

items.name: Trang Moo Yang
items.blurb: The legendary name for Trang roast pork, set in an old-school traditional coffee house. The signature is roast pork with crisp, fragrant skin that they roast themselves every day. Beyond the pork there's a fried spring roll made to their own recipe that's hard to find elsewhere, plus several kinds of dim sum. A great place to sit down for a full breakfast all in one shop.
items.price: Roast pork THB 20–40/100g · dim sum THB 20–35/basket

items.name: Pong Ocha 2
items.blurb: A dim sum and roast pork spot that locals rate as one of the best in town. Branch 2 is the big one with a wide menu: lots of dim sum baskets, roast pork by the plate, baked pork rib rice, and traditional coffee. It opens at 5:30 a.m. and fills up in the morning, so get there before 8 to sit comfortably.
items.price: THB 20–35 per basket · around THB 80–150 per person

items.name: Khao Ocha (Ko Khao Bao Buns)
items.blurb: An old Chinese shop where the things to order are the roast pork and the steamed buns. There's also dim sum, sticky-rice bak chang, and several other Chinese breakfast dishes. Locals eat here regularly and you can fill up comfortably for under a hundred baht a head. Another spot locals recommend for solid crisp-skin roast pork.

blocks.title: Local tip
blocks.html: The crispest-skinned roast pork is usually the first batch out of the oven at the crack of dawn. If you want skin that's crackly rather than chewy, go before 8 a.m. and order the roast pork before anything else, because the good stuff sells out fast.

blocks.text: Pre-Dawn Dim Sum — Paired with Roast Pork and Tea

blocks.html: Dim sum in Trang is tied to the rhythm of rubber tappers who wake before dawn, so the tea shops open while the sky is still dark. Order a hot tea, two or three baskets of dim sum, and you're full fast for little money. The standouts are roast-pork buns, shrimp har gow, siu mai, and crab rolls. If you want a full sit-down dim sum spread, Trang has plenty of options to choose from — see the full rundown in our Trang dim sum article.

items.name: Le Trang Dim Sum
items.blurb: One of the most popular dim sum spots in town, known for dim sum made fresh by hand, new each day, with baskets steaming on display out front. The standouts are roast-pork buns, big shrimp har gow, and crab rolls. Weekends get packed, so go early to skip a long wait.

items.name: Jeeb Khao
items.blurb: A tea shop in a shophouse over 80 years old, with a retro feel true to the original kopitiam style. The signature is the white siu mai, wrapped so it comes out translucent like har gow. There's also steamed buns, noodles, coffee and Chinese breakfast. Good for anyone who wants to experience a genuinely old Trang tea house.

items.name: Chen Jia Dim Sum Cafe
items.blurb: Hong Kong-style dim sum in a nicely done contemporary Chinese space. The shop is clean and comfortable to sit in, with standouts like Sichuan-sauce shrimp dumplings, salted-egg lava buns, and bak kut teh. Good for anyone who wants coffee alongside dim sum in a relaxed setting, and prices start reasonable.

blocks.text: Traditional Coffee and Kopi Shops — the Heart of a Trang Morning

blocks.html: A kopi shop is a traditional Chinese coffee house that's been the meeting point for Trang locals for decades. The coffee here is dark-roasted robusta brewed through a cloth filter, sweetened with condensed milk or sugar for a rich, sweet, creamy taste. Older folks come to sip coffee, read the news, and talk rubber prices. Many kopi shops also serve dim sum, roast pork and breakfast, so one stop gets you both the coffee and the food.

items.name: Kopi Sombat
items.blurb: A hugely popular kopi shop with both locals and travelers, and it genuinely opens in the pre-dawn dark. The menu covers everything from congee, dim sum and youtiao to dark traditional coffee. The youtiao here is something a lot of people recommend ordering. The atmosphere is classic coffee-house and it buzzes in the morning.

items.name: Kopi Sathani
items.blurb: A traditional coffee house open for more than 30 years, near Trang railway station — turn right out of the station and walk about 100–150 metres. It serves traditional coffee, dim sum and breakfast. Recommended orders are the well-stuffed buns, bak kut teh with mantou, and baked pork rib rice. Sip a kopi or an iced black coffee and soak up the real local vibe.

items.name: Kopi Mueang Trang
items.blurb: An old coffee house that's been part of Trang for over 80 years (since 1942) and was once a hangout for teens in the '70s and '80s. The atmosphere is authentic kopitiam, with traditional coffee, hot tea and dim sum-style breakfast. Better suited to people who want to sit and absorb a legendary tea house than to those after photos.

blocks.title: Know before you order
blocks.html: A few southern Thai coffee terms worth knowing: kopi is hot coffee with milk, oliang is iced black coffee with sugar, kopi-o is hot black coffee, and hot tea is called teh. Order the right one and you'll get exactly the cup you want.

blocks.text: Morning Markets — Everything in One Place

blocks.html: If you can't decide what to eat, head to a morning market and settle it in one place. There's sliced roast pork bagged to go, dim sum, youtiao, coffee, southern fruit, and local snacks lined up in a row. Graze your way along and soak up the sight of Trang waking up early at the same time.

items: Trang Municipal Fresh Market — a big market in the centre of town with sliced roast pork to go, dim sum, khanom jeen, fruit, and a full spread of breakfast food. Good for buying and finding a seat to eat nearby.

Si Trang Market — a morning market locals know well, with small tea shops, coffee, dim sum and steamed buns at easy prices. It's a real morning market rather than a dressed-up pretty spot, but you get the original flavours.
Markets in your neighbourhood — nearly every area has its own morning market. Ask your hotel where the nearest one is; you'll usually find food that's cheaper and fresher than in the malls.

blocks.html: If you have two mornings in Trang, try it like this: day one for the full legendary spread, day two for traditional coffee and a relaxed morning market. You'll cover the roast pork, dim sum and kopi without rushing.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Roast Pork and a Table Full of Dim Sum

items.activity: Start at Trang Moo Yang. Order crisp-skin roast pork from the morning batch, with fried spring rolls and dim sum.
items.note: Go before 8 a.m. for the crispest skin.

items.activity: Walk it off in Trang's old town, taking in the Sino-Portuguese buildings and old shops along the way.
items.note: The old-town streets photograph well in the morning light.

items.activity: Follow up with dim sum at Le Trang. Order the big shrimp har gow and roast-pork buns.
items.note: Packed on weekends, so leave time to wait for the steamer.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Traditional Coffee and a Morning Market

items.activity: Start at Kopi Sombat. Order traditional coffee with youtiao and sip slowly, local style.
items.note: Opens in the pre-dawn dark; people trickle in before sunrise.

items.activity: Walk through Trang Municipal Fresh Market and grab a bag of sliced roast pork and some southern fruit to take with you.
items.note: The market is liveliest between 7 and 9 a.m.

items.activity: Wrap up at Kopi Sathani near the railway station. Order an iced oliang with a steamed bun.
items.note: If you're catching a train next, this spot is an easy walk to the station.

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: Many of Trang's legendary breakfast spots are cash only, open in the pre-dawn dark and close early around midday. Lines get long between 7 and 9 a.m., especially on weekends. Bring small bills and go early to make life easier — the crisp-skin roast pork and the best dim sum baskets tend to run out before mid-morning.

faq.q: What do Trang locals eat for breakfast?
faq.a: The classic Trang breakfast is Trang roast pork sliced onto a plate, eaten with hot dim sum straight from the steamer and cloth-filtered traditional coffee from a kopi shop. Some people add steamed buns, youtiao, or baked pork rib rice.

faq.q: What makes Trang roast pork special?
faq.a: Trang roast pork is a whole side of pork belly, marinated and roasted in a traditional oven until the skin puffs up crisp while the meat inside stays tender and juicy. Locals eat it for breakfast rather than as an evening snack, and it has earned GI status as one of the province's signature dishes.

faq.q: What time do Trang breakfast spots open?
faq.a: Tea shops and roast pork spots in Trang open very early, many from 5:30 a.m., such as Pong Ocha 2 and Kopi Sombat. Trang Moo Yang opens from 6 a.m. to early afternoon. The good stuff often sells out before noon, so going before 8 a.m. is recommended.

faq.q: What are Trang's traditional coffee and kopi shops?
faq.a: A kopi shop is a traditional Chinese coffee house that has long been a meeting point for Trang locals. The coffee is dark-roasted robusta brewed through a cloth filter with condensed milk or sugar for a rich, sweet, creamy taste. Well-known spots include Kopi Sombat, Kopi Sathani and Kopi Mueang Trang, which has been open for over 80 years.

faq.q: What's a reasonable budget for a Trang local breakfast?
faq.a: About THB 100–180 per person gets you a full spread — say 100g of roast pork, 3–4 baskets of dim sum, plus a traditional coffee. If you go light with just coffee and a steamed bun or youtiao, it's much cheaper.
